reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: An inherited disorder of bile acid handling characterised by markedly raised serum bile acids (hypercholanaemia) with pruritus and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
Serum gamma-glutamyl transferase is typically low or normal, distinguishing it from obstructive cholestasis
Described in genetically isolated Amish kindreds and linked to variants in genes including TJP2, BAAT, and EPHX1
Clinical severity varies from asymptomatic elevation of bile acids to itch, steatorrhoea, and coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency
Growth may be impaired because of fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
The defects impair either tight-junction integrity of the biliary canaliculus or bile acid conjugation/transport, raising circulating unconjugated or poorly conjugated bile acids
Management is supportive with ursodeoxycholic acid, fat-soluble vitamin replacement, and antipruritic measures
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hypercholanaemia is a genetically heterogeneous condition in which serum bile acid concentrations are elevated without the biochemical hallmarks of biliary obstruction. Reported causes include mutations in TJP2 (tight junction protein 2), which compromises the paracellular barrier of the bile canaliculus; BAAT (bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase), which impairs conjugation of bile acids with glycine and taurine; and EPHX1 (microsomal epoxide hydrolase), affecting hepatocellular bile acid transport. The net effect is disturbed enterohepatic recirculation with raised circulating bile acids, itch, and malabsorption of dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins, characteristically with a low or normal gamma-glutamyl transferase.
additionalDifferentials: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (especially low-GGT types)
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (in affected adults)
additionalInvestigations: Fasting serum total bile acid concentration
Gamma-glutamyl transferase and full liver function tests (characteristically low/normal GGT)
Fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E) and coagulation profile for vitamin K status
Genetic testing of TJP2, BAAT, and EPHX1
Assessment of growth and nutritional status
Liver biopsy in atypical or progressive cases
redFlags: Progressive itch with sleep disturbance and skin excoriation
Evolving chronic liver disease in TJP2-related cases
reference.prognosis: Many individuals have a benign course with elevated bile acids and manageable symptoms, but pruritus and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency can be troublesome, and certain genotypes (particularly TJP2-related disease) carry a risk of progressive liver injury.
pitfalls: Interpreting a normal GGT as excluding significant cholestasis
Missing vitamin K deficiency as a cause of bleeding
Overlooking the diagnosis in isolated or consanguineous populations
Assuming a uniformly benign outcome despite genotype-dependent progression
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Suchy, Sokol & Balistreri, Liver Disease in Children
management: Ursodeoxycholic acid to improve bile acid handling and reduce pruritus
Antipruritic therapy with a bile acid sequestrant such as cholestyramine and/or rifampicin for troublesome itch
Fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) supplementation with correction of vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy
Nutritional support using medium-chain triglyceride-based feeds to counter fat malabsorption and support growth
Monitoring of growth, fat-soluble vitamin status, coagulation and liver function
Genetic counselling with testing of TJP2, BAAT and EPHX1 and family screening
Hepatology follow-up with vigilance for progressive liver injury, particularly in TJP2-related disease
